title: Lehmann’s inner core
teaches: Faint waves inside the shadow zone, the solid inner core they revealed, and how its growth powers the magnetic field

blocks.text: Inge Lehmann trained as a mathematician in Copenhagen and in 1928 became head of the seismology department of Denmark's new Geodetic Institute, responsible for the country's seismograph stations in Denmark and Greenland. Much of her work was the routine of reading records and measuring arrival times. She kept her notes on cardboard cards, sorted in oatmeal boxes.

On 17 June 1929 a large earthquake struck near Murchison, in the northern South Island of New Zealand. New Zealand is almost directly opposite Europe on the globe, so most European stations lie between about 140° and 180° from it, measured as an angle at the Earth's centre: beyond the far edge of the core's shadow, where the waves that arrive have crossed the core (lesson D4). Studying those records, and others from stations closer to the quake, Lehmann noticed something that the standard picture did not allow. Faint P waves were arriving at distances inside the shadow zone, between about 104° and 140°, where no direct wave was supposed to land.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Lehmann ran the seismograph stations of Denmark and Greenland from 1928.
In records of the 1929 Murchison earthquake in New Zealand, she found faint P waves arriving inside the shadow zone.

blocks.text: Lehmann proposed a simple explanation in 1936, in a paper titled only "P′" (P-prime, the label seismologists then used for P waves that had passed through the core). Suppose the core has an inner part where waves travel faster: about 11 kilometres a second, against 8 to 10 in the liquid outer core. A wave that dives deep enough to reach this inner core speeds up there and is turned toward a flatter path, the opposite of what happens when a wave enters the slower outer core. Some waves are turned enough to come back out and land inside the shadow, and others bounce off the inner core's surface and land there too. They are faint, because only a narrow range of paths does this, so little of the earthquake's energy goes that way.

blocks.caption: The Earth from lesson D4, with the liquid outer core in place (P waves at 8 to 10 km/s). Add an inner core where P waves travel at about 11 km/s; paths drawn in rose are those that enter it.
blocks.task: Add an inner core at least 900 km in radius that sends waves into the shadow

blocks.text: Her model was deliberately simple: a core and an inner core, each with one constant speed throughout. Within a few years Beno Gutenberg and Charles Richter, and Harold Jeffreys, had confirmed the inner core with more records. Lehmann had put its edge at about 5,000 kilometres down; the modern figure is 5,150, which, with the Earth's radius of 6,371 kilometres, gives the inner core a radius of 1,220 kilometres, about 70 per cent of the Moon's radius.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Lehmann (1936) proposed an inner core where waves travel faster, bending some of them outward into the shadow zone.
The inner core's edge is 5,150 km down; it has a radius of 1,220 km.

blocks.text: A sudden jump in wave speed at the inner core's edge suggested a change of state, solid inside liquid, as Francis Birch argued in 1940. Waves passing through it are faint and hard to read, though, and proving it took until 1971. Very large earthquakes set the whole Earth ringing like a bell for days, at a set of exact frequencies that depend on the stiffness of every layer. Adam Dziewonski and Freeman Gilbert analysed the ringing after large earthquakes of the 1960s and showed that the inner core must be rigid: it is solid, almost certainly an alloy of iron and nickel like the core around it.

The temperature at the centre is over 5,000 °C, hotter than the outer core. The inner core is solid anyway because of pressure, which is more than three million times that at the surface. A liquid takes up a little more room than the same solid, so squeezing a substance favours the solid, and the higher the pressure, the hotter it must be to melt. Going down through the core, the melting point of iron rises faster than the temperature does. At 5,150 kilometres down, both are around 5,000 to 6,000 °C, and below that depth the iron is cooler than its melting point and freezes.

As the Earth slowly loses heat, more of the outer core freezes onto the inner core, which grows by perhaps a millimetre a year. Iron in the core is mixed with some lighter elements, probably oxygen, sulphur and silicon among them, and these stay in the liquid when iron freezes. Freezing releases heat, and it leaves the liquid just above the inner core lighter, so that it rises like oil through water. Both stir the outer core and help keep the molten iron churning, and that churning drives the magnetic field of lesson 9. The inner core is much younger than the Earth itself: estimates based on how fast heat flows out of the core put its age at between about half a billion and two billion years, and the number is still debated.
Lehmann worked on the Earth's interior for the rest of her long life. She continued to publish into her nineties, and died in 1993 at 104.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Dziewonski and Gilbert (1971) showed from the Earth's ringing after great earthquakes that the inner core is solid.
Pressure raises the melting point of iron faster than the temperature rises with depth, so the centre is solid though hotter than the outer core.
The inner core grows as the outer core freezes onto it, which helps power the magnetic field.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the inner core
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why were the faint waves Lehmann saw surprising?
choices: They arrived inside the shadow zone, where no direct P wave was supposed to land
They arrived before the earthquake happened
They were S waves that had crossed the liquid core
items.why: The core's shadow was expected to be empty of direct P waves between about 104° and 140°.

items.ask: How does an inner core send waves into the shadow?
choices: Waves speed up in it and are bent outward, so some emerge at distances inside the shadow
It reflects all waves straight back to the quake
It slows waves until they stop
items.why: Entering faster material bends a wave away from the steeper direction, the opposite of what the slower outer core does.

items.ask: Why is the inner core solid when it is hotter than the liquid outer core?
choices: The pressure there raises iron's melting point above the temperature
It is made of rock, not iron
It is cooled by the outer core
items.why: With depth the melting point rises faster than the temperature. Below 5,150 km the iron is cooler than its melting point, so it is solid.

items.ask: How was the inner core shown to be solid in 1971?
choices: From the frequencies at which the whole Earth rings after great earthquakes
From the colour of volcanic lava
items.why: The Earth's ringing depends on the stiffness of every layer. Dziewonski and Gilbert found the inner core must be rigid.

items.ask: How does the growing inner core help the magnetic field?
choices: Freezing releases heat and light elements that stir the liquid outer core, which generates the field
The solid inner core is a permanent magnet
It blocks the Sun's magnetic field
items.why: The field comes from moving, conducting liquid iron. Freezing at the inner core's surface helps keep it moving.

learned: Lehmann (1936) explained faint P waves in the shadow zone with a faster inner core.
The inner core, 1,220 km in radius, is solid iron and nickel, shown in 1971 from the Earth's ringing.
Pressure keeps the centre solid though it is over 5,000 °C, and the freezing inner core helps power the magnetic field.
